note: Read from tree-sitter-scala's scanner.c, and the reading corrects a first
guess that was wrong in an instructive way.
Every misread byte scala has is the word `else` - twenty of them, eighty
bytes, and nothing else on the board. The obvious suspect is that six of
scala's externals are declared as bare STRING literals (`else` `catch`
`finally` `extends` `derives` `with`) rather than symbols. That is a red
herring twice over: the C never emits any of them (there is no
`result_symbol = ELSE` in it - they are in `externals` only so the scanner can
ASK whether one is expected), and press already interns such an entry as the
ordinary literal it also is, so `else` is a perfectly lexable terminal here.
The actual wall is one symbol upstream. `_if_body` spells the tail as
`_control_tail_gate` then `'else'`, so the state that shifts `else` is only
reachable through a ZERO-WIDTH external - and that external was blind. With no
gate the parse never reaches the two states where `else` shifts (`joints state
--census else`: sole shift, no rivals), so at `1 else 2` the only admitted
reading is scala's infix-operator rule and `else` comes back `identifier`. The
keyword rule never fired because there was no tie to break.
The gate needs no memory at all - it is the next word and the permission set -
which is why it is one rule and why it was worth reading past the first guess.
scala's real memory (the typed indent stack with its CASE_INDENT_FLAG, and the
registers around it) belongs to INDENT/OUTDENT/COMMA_OUTDENT, which the troupe
hands answer today with no misread bytes to show for it. Those move when rung 4
moves them; there is no board movement to buy there first.

rules.name: control_tail_gate
rules.note: scanner.c:1650-1673, the general arm. Three earlier paths emit the same token under narrower cover - the indent probe at 1014 (a block cannot open on a tail keyword), the `catch` remainder at 1643, and the semicolon machinery at 1256-1305 - and all four reduce to: the gate is wanted, the next word is a tail word, emit zero width. The C's own arms differ only in which tail words they list, and the widest list is this one. `then` and `yield` are gated the same as the block-closing three; `do` and `while` are deliberately not, because they can start a statement and gate validity blends in from unrelated GLR forks. The blanks are in the probe because the C reaches every one of those arms through a prologue that has already skipped them, and the tail may sit on its own line under a lesser indentation (`if (isEmpty)\n  (None, None)\nelse {`) - which is both remaining misread byte on this corpus. Crossing a newline to answer is the C's own preference too: at 1256 the gate is returned from *inside* the AUTOMATIC_SEMICOLON arm, so a tail keyword beats the semicolon it would otherwise insert. A comment between the two is not skipped, which narrows the rule rather than widening it.
